citation: Zhu et al. (2026), Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience
title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults, with reference to chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia.
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization), mentions psychological constructs (catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, depression), and minimally addresses social factors (social isolation, family support). Integration is directional between bio and psych, but triadic integration is partial.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychological factors (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) directionally amplify central sensitization (bio-psych). Social factors are mentioned as outcomes or comorbidities but not mechanistically linked. Triadic integration is partial: the BPS definition includes bio and psych but omits social.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but defines it as bio-psych only, omitting social
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological domain is elaborated with multiple mechanisms, while social domain is minimal and not integrated
conceptual_tensions_3: The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces geroscience as a new lens for MPS, but this is primarily biological, not biopsychosocial
additional_observations_2: Digital therapeutics are presented as a way to scale psychological interventions, but social barriers (digital divide) are acknowledged
additional_observations_3: The case example illustrates real-world gaps in multidisciplinary care, but the framework remains largely theoretical
synthesis_note: This narrative review proposes a geroscience-informed BPS framework for geriatric MPS. It elaborates biological mechanisms (sarcopenia, inflammaging, central sensitization) but treats psychological constructs as modulators without mechanistic depth. Social factors are minimally addressed. The BPS label is used as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, but triadic integration is partial: bio-psych integration is directional, while social is loosely attached. The paper contributes a geroscience lens but does not substantively operationalize the full BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and triadic integration is partial. Bio-dominant balance reflects the elaborated biological content. Integration is directional for bio-psych, mentioned for others.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as an organizing principle to group predictors into three domains. It does not define the model formally, nor does it specify mechanisms linking domains. Social factors are treated as proxies of illness behavior rather than classical social determinants.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper notes associations between biological and psychological factors (e.g., pain intensity and catastrophizing) and between psychological and social proxies (e.g., healthcare-seeking and distress), but no mechanistic pathways are specified.

additional_observations_2: The GRADE assessment downgraded evidence for sleep-related and occlusal factors to very low, indicating limited empirical support for those lifestyle factors
synthesis_note: This review uses the BPS model as a post-hoc organizing framework for grouping predictors but does not integrate domains. No mechanistic cross-domain pathways are proposed.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because all three domains are named but social is thin and no integration is present. Triadic integration is none because domains are listed in parallel. Psych-dominant balance reflects the elaborated psychological content.

title: Acceptance of pain neuroscience education in chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions: qualitative systematic review
authors: Lukas Kühn; Eileen Wengemuth; Lara Kleist; Kyung Eun (Anna) Choi
pain_condition_detail: chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions including chronic low back pain, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, neck pain, rheumatoid arthritis
bps_function_set: background framing; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label to frame PNE as addressing biopsychosocial etiology, but the review itself focuses on qualitative determinants of PNE acceptance. Biological content is limited to neurophysiology education topics; psychological content includes kinesiophobia, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression; social content is minimal (clinician-patient relationship, professional culture). No integration across domains is proposed.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper mentions that trust may modulate neural pain processing and that biomedical beliefs may cause skepticism, but no cross-domain pathway or mechanism is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal tool for qualitative research

conceptual_tensions_3: Psychological constructs (kinesiophobia, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression) are named but never defined or operationalized
additional_observations_1: The review is a qualitative meta-aggregation of determinants of PNE acceptance, not a review of BPS model operationalization. BPS is used as a descriptor for PNE content, not as an analytic framework
additional_observations_2: The paper's main contribution is identifying barriers and facilitators to PNE implementation, not testing or elaborating the BPS model
synthesis_note: This qualitative systematic review uses the biopsychosocial label to frame PNE as addressing biopsychosocial etiology, but the review itself does not operationalize or integrate the three domains. Biological content is limited to neurophysiology topics taught in PNE; psychological constructs are named but undefined; social content is minimal. The paper's contribution is to PNE implementation, not to BPS model testing.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no integration occurs. Triadic integration is none. Psychological domain dominates as the main analytic thread.

title: Biopsychosocial predictive factors for developing chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement surgery: A systematic review

bps_function_set: conclusion; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing principle to structure the review of predictive factors into biological, psychological, and socioeconomic categories. It lists factors within each domain but does not define the model or specify cross-domain mechanisms. Integration is limited to mentioning multiple domains in the same narrative.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper notes that the association between neuropathic-like pain and CPSP disappeared after adjusting for central sensitization and pain catastrophizing, suggesting shared variance but no mechanism is specified. Socio-economic disadvantages are theorized to affect coping strategies and social support, but no pathway is detailed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label to structure the review but does not define the model or specify how domains interact
conceptual_tensions_2: Social factors are acknowledged as important but only one study reported on education, leaving the social domain largely unexamined
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper lists multiple risk factors in parallel without proposing a mechanism for how they combine or interact
additional_observations_1: The paper's primary contribution is a systematic catalog of predictive factors for CPSP after THA, organized by BPS domains, but it does not integrate the domains beyond listing them
additional_observations_2: The paper uses the term 'biopsychosocial' in the abstract, methods, discussion, and conclusion, but never defines what the model means or how it should be operationalized
additional_observations_3: The paper acknowledges the complexity of CPSP but does not propose a testable model or pathway linking the identified factors
synthesis_note: This systematic review uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing principle to catalog predictive factors for chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement. It provides a thorough list of biological and psychological factors but minimal social content. The domains are listed in parallel with no cross-domain mechanisms proposed, making it a multifactorial rather than integrative use of the BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but treated in parallel. Triadic integration is 'none' because no three-domain mechanism or narrative is proposed. Social domain is 'minimal' because only education and race are briefly mentioned. The paper uses BPS language extensively but does not define or integrate the model.

integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes directional links: minority stress leads to HPA axis dysregulation and central sensitization; anxiety/depression amplify pain sensitivity via shared neural circuits; discrimination predicts chronic pain. No mechanistic pathway is specified for any link; triadic integration is descriptive.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS as an organizing principle but biological content is thin (hormones, sensitization) compared to psychological and social content
conceptual_tensions_2: Integration is asserted as 'interplay' but no mechanistic pathways are specified, factors are listed in parallel
conceptual_tensions_3: Gender-affirming care is presented as both a protective factor and a potential source of pain (e.g., chest binding), creating a tension not fully resolved
additional_observations_1: The paper applies the Minority Stress Model extensively, which is a social-psychological framework, but does not integrate it with biological mechanisms beyond HPA axis dysregulation
additional_observations_2: No instruments or measures are named, the review is conceptual and narrative
additional_observations_3: The paper explicitly calls for longitudinal studies and participatory research, indicating awareness of evidence gaps
synthesis_note: This narrative review applies a BPS lens to chronic pain in TGD youth, elaborating psychological and social factors while biological content is limited to hormonal and sensitization concepts. Integration is directional and descriptive, not mechanistic. The paper contributes a minority stress framework but does not operationalize BPS beyond listing factors.
coding_rationale: Typology 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but treated in parallel with no mechanistic integration. Triadic integration 'descriptive' as interplay is asserted without pathways. Dyadic balance because psychological and social domains dominate.

title: Applicability of the theory of pain-sensorimotor interactions to orofacial pain and sensorimotor behavior, and implications for orofacial pain research and management
authors: Barry J. Sessle; Greg M. Murray
journal: Journal of Oral & Facial Pain and Headache
pain_condition_detail: Orofacial pain, including temporomandibular disorders (TMD), burning mouth syndrome (BMS), persistent dentoalveolar pain, trigeminal neuropathic pain
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as the foundational framework for TOPSMI, listing biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors that influence pain-sensorimotor interactions. It describes these factors as having 'mixes and weightings' that affect CNS plasticity and sensorimotor behavior, but does not operationalize them into specific variables or measures.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that psychosocial, genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors influence CNS plasticity (neuroplasticity and glioplasticity), which in turn affects sensorimotor behavior and pain. The social domain is mentioned but not mechanistically integrated; the primary pathway is bio-psych with social as a contextual modifier.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses 'psychosocial factors' as an umbrella term that conflates psychological (stress, anxiety) and social (economic factors, family environment) constructs without distinguishing them
conceptual_tensions_2: TOPSMI is presented as a mechanistic framework but the paper acknowledges it may be difficult to test as a whole due to the many factors involved
conceptual_tensions_3: Social domain is mentioned (sociocultural factors, socioeconomic status) but never elaborated with specific mechanisms, creating a gap between BPS rhetoric and actual coverage
additional_observations_1: The paper is primarily a biological review of orofacial pain-sensorimotor interactions, with psychological and social factors mentioned but not developed
additional_observations_2: The biopsychosocial model is used as a foundational framework for TOPSMI, but the paper does not operationalize any BPS components into specific variables or measures
additional_observations_3: The paper introduces the novel TOPSMI framework, which is an extension of the BPS model specifically for pain-sensorimotor interactions
additional_observations_4: Genetic and epigenetic factors are treated as biological factors, but the paper also notes they can be modified by psychosocial and environmental factors, suggesting a more complex interaction
synthesis_note: This paper applies the novel TOPSMI framework to orofacial pain, using the biopsychosocial model as its foundation. It provides an elaborated biological account of pain-sensorimotor interactions (nociceptive pathways, CNS plasticity, genetics, epigenetics) but treats psychological and social factors as listed influences without mechanistic depth. The social domain is particularly thin, mentioned only as 'sociocultural factors' without specific constructs or pathways. The paper acknowledges the potential unfalsifiability of TOPSMI.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and psychological constructs are only named. Triadic integration is partial: bio-psych integration is directional via CNS plasticity, but social is loosely attached. Bio-dominant balance reflects the paper's primary focus on biological mechanisms.

title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS), a chronic musculoskeletal pain condition characterized by localized or regional pain, taut bands, and myofascial trigger points.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to situate fascia within a multifactorial framework, but never defines the model. It lists biological (fascial pathology), psychological (stress, catastrophizing, maladaptive coping), and social (inactivity) factors in parallel without specifying mechanisms linking them, and the social domain is minimal.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fascial pathology generates nociceptive input leading to central sensitization (bio-psych directional). Psychological and social factors (stress, catastrophizing, inactivity) are asserted to amplify pain via neuroimmune pathways, but no specific mechanism is detailed. No three-domain mechanism is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but provides minimal social content (only 'inactivity' is named) and no definition of the BPS model
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological factors (fascial pathology) are elaborated in detail, while psychological factors are only named and social factors are nearly absent, creating an imbalance
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper lists biological, psychological, and social factors in parallel without specifying how they interact mechanistically, despite claiming an integrative model
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces a novel 'fascial-neurogenic route' as a distinct etiopathophysiological pathway alongside the traditional 'myogenic route', but does not integrate these with psychosocial factors
additional_observations_2: The paper uses the term 'biopsychosocial' as an organizing principle but never defines what the model means, and the social domain is limited to a single factor ('inactivity')
synthesis_note: This narrative review elaborates biological mechanisms of fascial pathology in myofascial pain syndrome but uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle without defining the model. Psychological factors are named but not defined, and social content is minimal. Integration is partial: biological and psychological domains are directionally linked via central sensitization, but no three-domain mechanism is proposed.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and psychological constructs are only named. Triadic integration is partial because bio-psych is directional but social is only mentioned alongside. Bio-dominant balance reflects the paper's focus on fascial mechanisms.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Pathological fascia demonstrates collagen cross-linking, fiber thickening, and densification, reducing mobility and elasticity.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: Biopsies of painful fascia reveal upregulation of cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and extracellular matrix remodeling enzymes.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Inflammatory mediators released within fascial tissues—such as prostaglandins, cytokines, neurotrophins, and growth factors—activate and sensitize nociceptors.
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: Prolonged nociceptive input from fascia may trigger dorsal horn hyperexcitability, alter descending inhibitory control, and induce cortical reorganization of somatosensory maps.

title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
pain_condition_detail: non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as pain in the lumbar region present for at least 3 months
context_note: Focused on industrialized Western countries; includes primary, secondary, and tertiary care settings.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as an organizing principle to scope social factors in CLBP. It defines social factors broadly as external influences, reclassifies some biological/psychological factors as socially shaped, and proposes a six-domain classification. No cross-domain mechanisms are specified; integration is absent.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes associations between social factors and psychological constructs (e.g., depression mediating social status and pain, stress mediating income and pain) but specifies no pathways or processes.
emergent_labels_4: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status
conceptual_tensions_1: Paper reclassifies biological/psychological factors as social (e.g., BMI, sleep) but does not specify mechanisms linking them to social determinants
conceptual_tensions_2: Claims BPS model involves 'complex interactions' but only lists social factors in parallel, no cross-domain integration is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: Acknowledges boundary issues between BPS domains but does not resolve them, uses broad definition of social factors that may dilute specificity
additional_observations_1: The paper is a scoping review that explicitly focuses on social factors, with minimal biological and psychological content. It uses BPS as an organizing principle to justify its scope but does not integrate domains
additional_observations_2: The classification system (six domains) is the main contribution, it is descriptive and does not propose causal pathways
additional_observations_3: The paper critiques the literature for treating social factors as adjustment variables rather than explanatory ones, but does not itself model them as such
synthesis_note: This scoping review provides a comprehensive classification of social factors in CLBP (28 categories, 6 domains) but does not integrate biological, psychological, and social domains. BPS is used as an organizing principle; no mechanisms or pathways are specified. The paper is social-dominant with minimal biological and psychological coverage, illustrating a common pattern of BPS language without substantive integration.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but biological and psychological domains are thin. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are listed in parallel. Social domain is elaborated; biological and psychological are minimal/mentioned.

title: Social dimensions as explanatory approaches for the development of chronic pain: a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies
authors: Sarah Potthoff; Dominik Koesling; Claudia Bozzaro
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health

context_note: Studies from Canada, USA, UK, Australia, Norway, Sweden, Spain, Germany, Chile, Ethiopia, Switzerland, Jordan, worldwide online; focus on marginalized groups.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; critique or problematization
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as background framing to justify focusing on the neglected social dimension. It does not operationalize BPS itself; instead, it critiques the model for lacking theoretical foundations in social analysis and conducts a meta-ethnography exclusively on social dimensions, leaving biomedical and psychological aspects unanalyzed.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes associations between social factors (e.g., stigmatization, adversities, high expectations, loneliness) and chronic pain, but does not specify pathways or mechanisms linking social to psychological or biological domains.

conceptual_tensions_1: Paper critiques BPS for neglecting social dimension, but its own analysis also neglects biological and psychological domains, reproducing the same imbalance in reverse
conceptual_tensions_2: Lifestyle factors are categorized as a social dimension, but could also be considered individual behavioral or psychological factors, creating ambiguity
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper excludes studies that treat social as 'individual psychosocial phenomenon from a psychological perspective', yet some included social factors (e.g., stoicism, loneliness) have strong psychological components
additional_observations_1: The paper is a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies, not a systematic review of quantitative evidence, its contribution is conceptual and interpretive
additional_observations_2: The paper explicitly states it did not analyze additional study results beyond those related to social dimensions, meaning it deliberately excluded biological and psychological content from included studies
additional_observations_3: The paper uses BPS as a rhetorical foil to justify a single-domain (social) analysis, rather than operationalizing BPS as an integrative framework
synthesis_note: This meta-ethnography contributes a rich taxonomy of eight social dimensions (gender inequity, stigmatization, adversities, harsh conditions, high expectations, cultural beliefs, loneliness, lifestyle) as explanatory factors for chronic pain. However, it does not operationalize the biopsychosocial model integratively: biological and psychological domains are minimally present, and no cross-domain mechanisms are proposed. The paper critiques BPS for neglecting the social but reproduces the same imbalance by focusing exclusively on social factors.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but only the social domain is elaborated; biology and psychology are minimal. Triadic integration is none because domains are not related. Social-dominant balance reflects the paper's exclusive focus on social dimensions.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as a foundation for PIPT but focuses on bio (exercise, physical activity) and psycho (cognitive skill training) domains, explicitly noting that social factors are rarely addressed. integration_mechanism_summary: The model proposes that PIPT interventions (cognitive skill training + exercise) reduce pain-related disability through psychological mediators (psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, reduced catastrophizing/fear avoidance) and physical mediators (improved movement patterns). conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS as a foundation but explicitly notes that social factors are rarely addressed in BPS-labeled PT, creating a tension between the model's claim and its operationalization

conceptual_tensions_3: Psychological constructs like catastrophizing and fear avoidance are named but not formally defined, relying on assumed shared meaning
additional_observations_1: The paper proposes a logic model for PIPT that is explicitly designed to be culturally tailored, but the general model itself does not include social factors as essential intervention components
additional_observations_2: The paper's literature review on Latino populations provides rich social and cultural detail, but this is not integrated into the causal pathway of the logic model

The paper is valuable for its focus on cultural tailoring and its explicit identification of conceptual problems with BPS.

additional_observations_2: The paper identifies methodological heterogeneity in definitions and instruments as a limitation, which is relevant to operationalization of constructs
synthesis_note: This scoping review compares FM and LBP on pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes. It uses 'biopsychosocial' once in the abstract without definition or integration. citation: Bruti et al. (2024), Biomedicines
title: Insecure Attachment, Oxytocinergic System and C-Tactile Fibers: An Integrative and Translational Pathophysiological Model of Fibromyalgia and Central Sensitivity Syndromes
authors: Gianluca Bruti; Paola Foggetti; Alessandro Rimessi
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) and other central sensitivity syndromes (CSSs) such as migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic low back pain, complex regional pain syndrome, post-herpetic neuralgia
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework to integrate attachment system, C-tactile fibers, and oxytocinergic system dysfunction into a pathophysiological model of fibromyalgia and central sensitivity syndromes. It proposes a mechanistic pathway linking early attachment, CT fiber stimulation, and oxytocinergic programming to stress system dysregulation and central sensitization. The model is described narratively without formal operationalization of BPS domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a mechanistic pathway: insecure attachment and early stress lead to dysfunction of C-tactile fibers and oxytocinergic system, which dysregulates the HPA axis and autonomic nervous system, resulting in central sensitization and chronic pain. This integrates biological (CT fibers, OS, HPA) and psychological (attachment, stress) domains mechanistically, but social factors are only descriptively linked.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper proposes a mechanistic bio-psych model but social factors are only mentioned, not integrated mechanistically
conceptual_tensions_2: Oxytocinergic system dysfunction and insecure attachment are described as 'two sides of the same coin', conflating biological and psychological constructs without clear distinction
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label but the social domain is minimally developed, making the model effectively dyadic
conceptual_tensions_4: The proposed model is highly speculative and integrative but lacks empirical testing or operationalization of key constructs
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces a novel pathophysiological model integrating attachment theory, C-tactile fibers, and oxytocinergic system, but does not operationalize any of these constructs for measurement
additional_observations_2: The review is a narrative synthesis that cites empirical studies but does not conduct a systematic search or quality assessment

synthesis_note: This narrative review proposes an integrative pathophysiological model of fibromyalgia linking insecure attachment, C-tactile fiber dysfunction, and oxytocinergic system dysregulation to central sensitization. title: The emergence of sex differences in primary pain during adolescence: a conceptual developmentally-oriented biopsychosocial model and opportunities for further investigation
authors: Hannah Hagy; Esmeralda Hidalgo-Lopez; Christel Portengen; Alexis Holman; Andrew Schrepf; Daniel J. Clauw; Steven E. Harte; Adriene M. Beltz; Amy M. Bohnert; Chelsea M. Kaplan
pain_condition_detail: primary pain conditions including fibromyalgia, migraine/headache, temporomandibular disorder, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pelvic pain, multisite pain
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label to organize a narrative review of sex differences in primary pain during adolescence. It lists biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors as overlapping contributors, with brain network function as a central susceptibility factor. No empirical integration or testing of the model is performed.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that brain network function is a central susceptibility factor that interacts with overlapping biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors. Specific directional claims include hormones reorganizing brain regions and adverse events influencing pubertal timing. No mechanistic triadic pathway is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper lists biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors as overlapping but does not specify how they interact mechanistically
conceptual_tensions_2: Sex and gender are acknowledged as distinct but the paper largely focuses on sex due to its neurobiological focus, leaving the role of gender underexplored
conceptual_tensions_3: The model proposes brain network function as a central susceptibility factor, but the evidence for this is limited to one study in children prior to pain onset
additional_observations_1: The paper emphasizes the need for sex-stratified analyses and consideration of pubertal status, timing, and tempo in future research
additional_observations_2: The review is conceptual and not exhaustive, aiming to provide a broad overview rather than a systematic synthesis
synthesis_note: This conceptual review proposes a developmentally-oriented biopsychosocial model to explain sex differences in primary pain during adolescence. It provides a broad overview of biological, behavioral, cognitive-affective, and sociocultural factors, with a strong emphasis on brain network function and pubertal hormones. However, it does not empirically integrate these factors or specify mechanistic pathways, resulting in a multifactorial rather than integrative use of the BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but treated in parallel with no mechanistic integration. Triadic integration is partial because brain network function is linked to multiple factors but no specific pathway is specified. Bio-dominant due to extensive coverage of hormones, brain structure, and nociplastic mechanisms.

authors: Ioannis Mavroudis; Katerina Franekova; Foivos Petridis; Alin Ciobîca; Dăscălescu Gabriel; Emil Anton; Ciprian Ilea; Sotirios Papagiannopoulos; Dimitrios Kazis; Katalin Prokai-Tatrai

bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework for FND, describing it as an interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors. It does not operationalize the model into specific variables or mechanisms but invokes it to justify a multidisciplinary approach and to frame comorbidities as integral to FND.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that biological, psychological, and social factors interact in FND but does not specify a mechanistic pathway. It describes shared neural circuits linking biological and psychological domains, and trauma as a social factor influencing psychological outcomes. No full triadic mechanism is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial model but provides no mechanistic integration across all three domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Social factors are mentioned but not elaborated, the paper is psych-dominant despite BPS framing

additional_observations_1: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' as an explanatory framework but does not operationalize it into specific variables or mechanisms
additional_observations_2: The review is a narrative synthesis with a PRISMA flow diagram, but it is not a systematic review
additional_observations_3: Chronic pain is treated as a somatic comorbidity of FND rather than as a primary condition
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework for FND but does not operationalize it. Psychological content is elaborated, while biological and social domains are mentioned but not developed. No mechanistic integration across domains is provided. The paper is psych-dominant and the BPS label is used rhetorically.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is thin and no triadic integration is achieved. Triadic integration is partial because two domains (bio-psych) are directionally linked while social is loosely attached. Psychological content is elaborated, biological and social are mentioned.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework and intervention rationale, describing it as full integration of biological, psychological, and social components. additional_observations_2: The paper emphasizes patient expectations and therapeutic alliance as key psychological constructs but does not use any standardized instruments
additional_observations_3: The paper references the fear-avoidance model and misdirected problem-solving model but does not test or extend them
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses BPS as an organizing framework for geriatric pain management principles but operationalizes it primarily through psychological constructs (fear, avoidance, expectations, self-efficacy, therapeutic alliance). Biological and social factors are mentioned but not elaborated. Integration is partial: directional links between fear and deconditioning, and between expectations and outcomes, but no triadic mechanism.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used extensively but social domain is thin and integration is partial. Triadic integration is partial because bio-psych and psych-social links are directional but bio-social is only mentioned. Psych-dominant balance reflects the paper's focus on psychological constructs.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS in its methods or analysis. The review scopes existential interventions and does not measure or integrate biological, psychological, and social factors.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that existential therapy may reduce pain by decreasing pain sensitivity or reducing negative evaluation of pain, linking psychological intervention to biological outcomes. No social or triadic mechanisms are proposed.

additional_observations_3: Social factors are virtually absent, only 'existential isolation' is mentioned, and no social determinants, support, or context are discussed
synthesis_note: This scoping review uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS. It focuses on psychological and existential/spiritual factors, with minimal biological and social content. Integration is limited to directional claims linking existential therapy to pain reduction. The paper contributes to the existential therapy literature but not to BPS operationalization.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no triadic integration occurs. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are not related. Psych-dominant due to heavy focus on psychological and existential constructs.

citation: Granger et al. (2025), Journal of Clinical Medicine
title: Pain Neuroscience Education on Reducing Opioid Dependency in African American and Caucasian Populations: A Narrative Review
authors: Austin Granger; Ersilia Mirabelli; Masahiro Kohzuki
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain conditions including chronic low back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with focus on nociplastic pain
context_note: US-focused review on African American and Caucasian populations in the context of the opioid epidemic.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework and intervention rationale, linking biological (neuroplasticity, nociplastic pain), psychological (pain catastrophizing, self-efficacy, fear), and social (ethnic disparities, healthcare access, trust) factors in a narrative synthesis, but without formal integration or testing of mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that maladaptive neuroplasticity (biological) and ethnic disparities in prescribing access and pain beliefs (psychosocial) intersect to influence opioid use, but no specific pathway or mediator is detailed for the triadic claim.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper asserts a triadic BPS framework but does not specify mechanisms linking biological, psychological, and social domains beyond co-occurrence
conceptual_tensions_2: The term 'faulty pain cognitions' is used broadly without clear definition or operationalization
conceptual_tensions_3: Social support is identified as important but the paper notes a lack of research on its role in OUD treatment outcomes
additional_observations_1: The paper uniquely integrates general systems theory and ecological systems theory as meta-frameworks for the BPS model
additional_observations_2: The review is a narrative synthesis without systematic search or quality appraisal, limiting its evidentiary weight
additional_observations_3: The paper calls for future research incorporating readiness-to-change models and neuroimaging to study ethnic differences in PNE response
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses BPS as an organizing framework to link neuroplasticity, psychological factors, and ethnic disparities in opioid use, but integration remains descriptive rather than mechanistic. The paper is notable for its explicit use of systems theories and its focus on ethnocultural factors, but lacks formal definition of key psychological constructs and does not specify cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are substantively present but treated in parallel without mechanistic integration. Triadic integration is descriptive: the paper asserts intersection but no pathway. Close call on social domain: elaborated due to detailed discussion of ethnic disparities, healthcare access, and trust.

citation: Young et al. (2025), Biology
title: Neurobiology of Chronic Pain, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
authors: Gerald Young; Hella Thielen; Kristin Samuelson; Joel Jin; Ioannis Mavroudis; Dimitrios A. Kazis
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (including chronic low back pain, chronic widespread pain, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, nociplastic pain), mild traumatic brain injury/concussion, posttraumatic stress disorder
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as a broad heuristic framework to contextualize sensitization mechanisms across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD. It places central/peripheral sensitization within the biological component and notes possible exacerbation from psychological and social factors, but does not operationalize or integrate the three domains substantively.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that psychological and social factors can exacerbate central/peripheral sensitization, but no pathway or mediator is specified. The fear-avoidance model is applied to MTBI sensory hypersensitivity, but not empirically tested. No triadic mechanism is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper defines BPS as a 'compendium' but also claims it as an explanatory framework, creating a tension between listing and integration
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper asserts that psychological and social factors exacerbate sensitization but provides no mechanism or pathway for this interaction
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses the fear-avoidance model for MTBI sensory hypersensitivity but notes it has not been empirically tested in that population
conceptual_tensions_4: The paper proposes a sensitization model as a common mechanism across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD, but the evidence for sensitization in MTBI and PTSD is largely theoretical
additional_observations_1: The paper is primarily a neurobiological review of chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD, with the BPS model used as a broad heuristic framework rather than an operationalized model
additional_observations_2: The paper introduces novel concepts (psychological reserve, psychological control, activation–inhibition coordination) but does not integrate them with the BPS model in a substantive way
additional_observations_3: The paper's sensitization model is the main integrative effort, but it focuses on biological mechanisms and only mentions psychological/social factors as potential exacerbators
additional_observations_4: The paper does not cite Engel (1977/1980) or any foundational BPS source, the model is attributed to Young's own synthesis
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial model as a broad heuristic to contextualize a neurobiological review of sensitization across chronic pain, MTBI, and PTSD. Biological content is elaborated, psychological content is mentioned, and social content is minimal. The BPS label is used for background framing and as an organizing principle, but no three-domain integration is achieved. The paper defines BPS as a 'compendium' and does not operationalize it.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no triadic integration is present. Triadic integration is 'none' because the paper only asserts that psychological and social factors can exacerbate biological sensitization without specifying any pathway. Bio-dominant balance reflects the paper's primary focus on neurobiology.

bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label to frame PRT as an intervention that implements the model in practice. integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a bidirectional fear-pain cycle (bio-psych) where fear amplifies central sensitization. conceptual_tensions_2: The term 'noziplastischer Schmerz' is central but its definition relies on exclusion of other mechanisms rather than positive criteria
additional_observations_1: The paper is a narrative review describing a specific therapy (PRT) rather than a systematic review of the BPS model
additional_observations_2: The social domain is reduced to a single mention of 'soziale Aspekte' without any specific constructs, mechanisms, or interventions
additional_observations_3: The paper uses fMRI evidence to support bio-psych integration but does not discuss social factors in the same empirical framework
synthesis_note: This paper uses the BPS label to frame PRT as an intervention that implements the model, but operationalizes it almost entirely through biological (central sensitization, neuroplasticity) and psychological (fear, catastrophizing, self-efficacy) mechanisms. additional_observations_1: The paper is primarily a narrative review about XR technology for neurocognitive training, not a systematic review of biopsychosocial factors
additional_observations_2: The psychological content is limited to naming neurocognitive domains (attention, memory, executive function) without defining them or linking them to pain mechanisms
additional_observations_3: No social factors are discussed, despite the BPS label being used multiple times
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial label as a background framing for chronic pain but does not operationalize any of its domains. title: Beyond the Biomedical Model: A Critical Review of the Approach to Chronic Pain and the Proposal of an Integrated Functional Model
authors: Alexander Muacevic; John R Adler; Luigi Pianese; Bruno Bordoni
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain, including chronic low back pain, chronic headache, migraine, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pelvic pain.
bps_function_set: conclusion; critique or problematization; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper critiques the BPS model for neglecting nutrition, environment, and lifestyle, and proposes extending it with a 'functional dimension' focused on the extracellular matrix as biological terrain. It does not operationalize BPS through specific variables or measures but uses it as a conceptual foil for proposing a new model.
integration_mechanism_summary: No cross-domain pathways are specified. The paper asserts that biological, psychological, and social factors interact but provides no mechanistic links. The proposed functional model focuses on biological terrain and lifestyle, not on integration.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper critiques the BPS model for neglecting nutrition and environment, yet its own proposed model adds a 'functional dimension' that is largely biological, not truly integrative
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper claims all pain is 'real' and multidimensional, but its proposed model focuses heavily on biological terrain, potentially marginalizing psychological and social factors
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses the BPS label extensively but does not define it beyond Engel's citation, and its critique is based on perceived gaps rather than on empirical evidence of BPS model failure
additional_observations_1: The paper is a narrative review with no systematic search strategy, no quality assessment, and no explicit inclusion criteria
additional_observations_2: The paper proposes a 'bio-psycho-functional-social model' but does not specify how the four dimensions interact mechanistically
additional_observations_3: The paper cites evidence for dietary and environmental influences on pain but does not integrate these with psychological or social mechanisms
additional_observations_4: The paper's critique of the BPS model is based on its perceived neglect of nutrition and environment, not on a systematic analysis of BPS literature
synthesis_note: This narrative review critiques the BPS model for neglecting nutrition, environment, and lifestyle, and proposes a 'bio-psycho-functional-social' model centered on the extracellular matrix. It offers no integration of the three core domains and no operationalization of BPS. Its value is as a critique and proposal, not as an empirical synthesis.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but psychological and social domains are only mentioned, while biological and lifestyle domains are elaborated. Triadic integration is 'none' as no cross-domain pathways are specified. The paper is bio-dominant.

authors: Rocio de Diego-Cordero; Emilio Martin-Palomino; Alicia Aranda-Jerez; Jose Miguel Perez-Jimenez; Giancarlo Lucchetti

bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' and 'biopsychosocial–spiritual' as organizing labels to argue that pain assessment should include spirituality. It does not define the model's components or relate them; the BPS label frames the rationale for including a spiritual dimension alongside existing domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The only cross-domain claim is a directional association between spirituality/hope and inflammatory markers, with no mechanism specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper advocates for a biopsychosocial–spiritual model but only substantively addresses the spiritual domain, biological, psychological, and social domains are minimally covered
conceptual_tensions_2: Spirituality is defined both narrowly (deity/higher power) and broadly (meaning/purpose), but the paper does not resolve which definition should guide assessment
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper critiques existing scales for 'contaminated' items that overlap with mental health, yet it does not propose a clean operationalization of spirituality distinct from psychological well-being
additional_observations_1: The paper is a scoping review of instruments, not a review of pain mechanisms or treatments, its BPS use is primarily to justify including spirituality as a domain
additional_observations_2: The only cross-domain integration claim (spirituality/hope → lower cytokines) is cited from other work, not from the reviewed instruments
additional_observations_3: The paper's main contribution is identifying the gap in spiritual assessment in Spanish-language pain scales, not in operationalizing the BPS model
synthesis_note: This scoping review uses 'biopsychosocial–spiritual' as an organizing label to argue for including spirituality in pain assessment. It substantively covers the spiritual/existential domain (hope, meaning, suffering, faith) but gives minimal attention to biological, psychological, and social domains. No triadic integration is present; the only cross-domain claim is a cited directional association between spirituality/hope and inflammatory markers. The paper's main finding is that most Spanish-language pain scales lack direct spiritual items and those that exist are 'contaminated' by overlap with mental health constructs.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but only the spiritual domain is elaborated; biological, psychological, and social domains are minimal or absent. Triadic integration 'none' because no three-domain relationship is articulated. The paper's primary function is to advocate for spiritual inclusion, not to integrate the three core domains.

title: The mutually reinforcing dynamics between pain and stress: mechanisms, impacts and management strategies
authors: Nour Aboushaar; Natalia Serrano
pain_condition_detail: Recurrent tension-type headaches, back, neck, and shoulder pain; chronic pain broadly (fibromyalgia, migraine, osteoarthritis, chronic back pain, lower back pain)

integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a bidirectional vicious cycle between pain and stress driven by overlapping physiological (HPA axis, neuroplasticity, inflammation), cognitive (catastrophizing, hypervigilance), and social (support, SES) mechanisms. conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' to structure the review but does not define the model or specify how the domains interact mechanistically
additional_observations_1: The paper focuses on the bidirectional relationship between pain and stress, using the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework for overlapping mechanisms
additional_observations_2: Lifestyle factors (diet, physical activity, sleep, substance use) are elaborated as a separate domain, treated with similar depth to biological and psychological factors
additional_observations_3: The paper includes a case study to illustrate the vicious cycle, but the case study does not demonstrate integration of the three domains
additional_observations_4: No instruments or measurement tools are named, the paper is a narrative review with no empirical data
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the biopsychosocial label to structure a discussion of overlapping mechanisms between pain and stress. title: Integrated Approach to Chronic Pain—The Role of Psychosocial Factors and Multidisciplinary Treatment: A Narrative Review
authors: Irena Kovačević; Jadranka Pavić; Biljana Filipović; Štefanija Ozimec Vulinec; Boris Ilić; Davorina Petek; Cesar Fernández-de-las-Peñas

bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing principle and intervention rationale, describing it as a framework for multidisciplinary rehabilitation. It lists biological, psychological, and social factors but does not specify mechanisms linking them. The model is invoked to justify multidisciplinary treatment rather than to explain pain pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper asserts associations between social factors (support, SES, relationships) and pain outcomes, and between psychological factors (beliefs, distress) and pain, but does not specify pathways or mechanisms linking domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper advocates for a biopsychosocial model but provides no mechanism linking biological, psychological, and social domains, they are listed in parallel
conceptual_tensions_2: Social factors are acknowledged as important but are not elaborated beyond listing, the paper is psych-dominant in actual content
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' and 'multidisciplinary' almost interchangeably, conflating the model with the treatment approach
additional_observations_1: The paper is a narrative review with no systematic search or quality assessment, limiting the strength of its claims
additional_observations_2: The paper cites Engel's biopsychosocial model but does not engage with its theoretical depth or critiques
additional_observations_3: The paper mentions ICD-11 classification and IASP definition but does not integrate these into the BPS analysis
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the biopsychosocial label extensively to justify multidisciplinary treatment, but operationalizes it as a list of separate components. Psychological content is elaborated (beliefs, attitudes, coping), while biological and social factors are mentioned but not developed. No cross-domain mechanisms are proposed, and the triadic integration is absent. The paper contributes to the finding that BPS language is widespread while substantive integration is not.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because all three domains are present but social and biological are thin, and no integration is specified. Triadic integration is 'none' because domains are listed in parallel. Psych-dominant because psychological content occupies most of the results.

bps_usage_instances_01_usage_verbatim: The biopsychosocial model, proposed by Engel as an alternative to the biomedical approach, offers a comprehensive framework for understanding illness and health by incorporating biological, psychological, and social factors.
bps_usage_instances_01_note: Defines the model as a framework incorporating three domains.
bps_usage_instances_02_usage_verbatim: The biopsychosocial model is considered essential for effective pain treatment. It provides a framework for multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation, which integrates physical training and patient education (biological component), cognitive–behavioral treatment (psychological component), and discussions about issues in the work and social environments (social component).
bps_usage_instances_02_note: Operationalizes the model into multidisciplinary rehabilitation components.
bps_usage_instances_03_usage_verbatim: Chronic pain should be approached with a biopsychosocial model within a multidisciplinary treatment framework. This model addresses the complex interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors, offering a holistic strategy for effective pain management.
bps_usage_instances_03_note: Concludes that BPS model is necessary for chronic pain management.
bps_usage_instances_04_usage_verbatim: The biopsychosocial model encourages a holistic view of pain, considering all aspects of the patient's nature, from physiology to social relationships and mental awareness.
bps_usage_instances_04_note: Describes the model as holistic.
bps_usage_instances_05_usage_verbatim: Considering biological, psychological, and sociological factors, the biopsychosocial model of treatment becomes necessary in the treatment of chronic pain.
bps_usage_instances_05_note: States necessity of BPS model for treatment.
